author: Aseer Sohlvi, Faisalabad
title: A farewell gift as Dr. Ahmad leaves for Hajj
titleOriginal: نذرانہ الوداع حج — اسیر سوہلوی فیصل آباد
takeaway: Lucky are the lovers who set off to see the Prophet's city.
scene: This poem is by Aseer Sohlvi of Faisalabad, a friend of Dr. Ahmad. It was written as a farewell when Dr. Ahmad set out on Hajj. It mirrors the poem Dr. Ahmad himself wrote when his friend Saim Chishti left for Hajj (page 80).

original: بج حج والے کئی عاشق چمن یار دے درد دیوار چلے
شکر رب دا لکھ کروڑ واری کرن نیک ایہہ ونج بیوپار چلے
transliteration: Bann Hajj vaale kayi aashiq chaman-e-yaar de dar-o-deewaar chale
Shukar Rab da lakh karor vaari, karan nek eh vanj beopaar chale
translation: Becoming pilgrims, many lovers have set off for the doors and walls of the Beloved's garden.
Thank God a million times: they're off to make this good trade.
couplets.story: Many lovers of God are setting out on Hajj, heading for the holy places, the 'garden' of the Beloved. Thank God a million times! They're going to make the best 'trade' there is: giving up the world to get closer to God.

original: آتش ہجر والی لیکے وچہ سینے اوتھے کرن سینے ٹھنڈے ٹھار چلے
رونا کم فراق دے ماریاں دا روندے نین ویکھو زارو زار چلے
transliteration: Aatish-e-hijr vaali lai ke vich seene, othe karan seene thande thaar chale
Rona kam firaaq de maariyaan da, ronde nain vekho zaaro zaar chale
translation: Carrying the fire of separation in their chests, they're going there to cool their hearts.
Weeping is the work of those struck by separation: look, they go with eyes pouring tears.
couplets.story: They carry the burning ache of missing God and the Prophet, and they're going to Makkah and Madinah to soothe it. Look at them: they're crying as they go.

original: بادشاہ گداواں دا بھیس کر کے منگن سخی دے وچہ دربار چلے
نال شوق دے کٹ مسافتاں نوں سروں لاہ سارے بھار چلے
transliteration: Baadshaah gadaavaan da bhes kar ke mangan Sakhi de vich darbaar chale
Naal shauq de katt musaafataan nu, siron laah saare bhaar chale
translation: Kings dress up as beggars and go to ask at the court of the Generous One;
eagerly they cover the distances, having lifted every burden off their heads.
couplets.story: Even kings dress as humble beggars, in the plain white pilgrim's clothes, to ask God, the Most Generous, for His blessings. They travel eagerly, putting down all their worldly worries.

original: مرضاں والیاں پا شفاء لینی روگی ہجر دے جیہڑے بیمار چلے
کئی تڑفدے سہکدے ہین ایتھے کرماں والے نے کرن دیدار چلے
transliteration: Marzaan vaaliyaan paa shifaa laini, rogi hijr de jehre beemaar chale
Kayi tarafde sehkde hain ethe, karmaan vaale ne karan deedaar chale
translation: The sick will find their cure, those who set off ill with the sickness of separation.
Many stay here aching and gasping; the fortunate are going to see.
couplets.story: People who are 'sick' with longing will find their cure there. Many people stay behind, aching to go. Only the lucky ones get to make the journey.

original: نجتاں والیاں دے ستے لیکھ جاگے ویکھن آقا دا پاک دیار چلے
جیہڑے نال محبتاں بھرے سینے مستاں وانگ ہو کے مستوار چلے
transliteration: Nijataan vaaliyaan de sutte lekh jaage, vekhan Aaqa da paak dayaar chale
Jehre naal mohabbataan bhare seene, mastaan vaang ho ke mastvaar chale
translation: The sleeping fortunes of the blessed have woken up: they're off to see the Master's pure city,
those whose hearts are full of love, going along like people lost in ecstasy.
couplets.story: Their luck has woken up. They're going to see Madinah, the pure city of the Prophet, their 'Master'. Their hearts are so full of love that they walk along as if dizzy with joy.

original: لکھ لکھ مبارکاں حاجیاں نوں پین نوٹاں تے پھلاں دے ہار چلے
بھائی احمدؔ دے دوست بخت چمکے بھائیاں نال وداع کرن یار چلے
transliteration: Lakh lakh mubaarakaan haajiyaan nu, pain notaan te phullaan de haar chale
Bhaai Ahmad de dost, bakht chamke, bhaaiyaan naal vidaa karan yaar chale
translation: A hundred thousand congratulations to the pilgrims! Garlands of banknotes and flowers are placed on them.
Brother Ahmad's friends, their fortune shining, come along with his brothers to see him off.
couplets.story: Congratulations to the pilgrims! Friends put garlands of money and flowers around their necks, a South Asian custom. Brother Ahmad's friends and family all come to wish him well and say goodbye.

original: میرے آقا نوں میرا اسلام کہنا جیدوں عرضاں داذ کر اذ کار چلے
سوہنے سد لیا جنوں سدناں سی ایہہ آپ نے کرن دیدار چلے
transliteration: Mere Aaqa nu mera salaam kehna, jidon arzaan da zikr-azkaar chale
Sohne sadd liya jinhu saddnaa si, eh aap ne karan deedaar chale
translation: Give my salaam to my Master, when you present your prayers and remembrances;
the Beautiful One has called those He meant to call, and they're going to see Him themselves.
couplets.story: His friend asks Dr. Ahmad: when you're praying at the Prophet's resting place, please send him my greetings. The Prophet has 'called' these lucky people to visit him.

original: لوک اناں نوں ویکھ کے خوش ہوندے ویکھن اے پاک سرکار چلے
میرے جئے اسیر کئی وچہ دنیا رل کے اپنی عمر گزار چلے
transliteration: Lok inaan nu vekh ke khush honde, vekhan ae Paak Sarkaar chale
Mere jaye Aseer kayi vich duniya, rul ke apni umar guzaar chale
translation: People are delighted to see them going off to see the pure Master.
Many prisoners (aseer) like me spend their whole lives lost in this world.
couplets.story: Everyone is happy to see them leave for the Prophet's city. The writer ends humbly. He plays on his pen-name 'Aseer', which means 'prisoner': many people like him spend their whole lives trapped in worldly things and never make it.

deeper: This poem shows the warmth of devotion to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ (the 'Master', Aaqa) in the poet's circle. Kings dressing as beggars refers to the simple white garments (ihram) every pilgrim wears, which make rich and poor look the same before God. Asking a pilgrim to carry your salaam to the Prophet is a much-loved custom.
why: A beautiful picture of how a community sends off someone going on Hajj: garlands, tears, blessings and messages for the Prophet.
prompt: If you could send a message with someone going somewhere sacred to you, what would it be?
notes: Written by Aseer Sohlvi for Dr. Ahmad. The last line, at the top of page 107, plays on 'aseer' (prisoner).
